books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Harriet Beecher Stowe, Uncle Tom’s Cabin, 1852

stimulus.source_note: Harriet Beecher Stowe, Uncle Tom’s Cabin; or, Life Among the Lowly (Boston: John P. Jewett & Company, 1852), Chapter 40, "The Martyr". Public domain.
stimulus.text: The longest way must have its close — the gloomiest night will wear on to a morning. An eternal, inexorable lapse of moments is ever hurrying the day of the evil to an eternal night, and the night of the just to an eternal day.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: In this passage, Stowe’s image of night wearing on to morning most directly expresses her belief that

options.text: slavery’s days were numbered and justice would come.
the South would win the debate over slavery.
options.misconception: Stowe writes for the enslaved, not for their masters; her morning belongs to the just, and the evil faces an eternal night.

options.text: the novel’s story was purely invented and had no moral point.
options.misconception: The passage is a moral claim, not a disclaimer; Stowe closes her novel by judging slavery, not by calling it make-believe.

options.text: Northerners should stop reading about slavery.
options.misconception: Background from the books: Stowe wrote to make Northerners feel slavery’s cruelty; the passage urges them on, it does not send them away.

rationales.A: Night gives way to morning and the day of evil ends: Stowe promises that slavery will pass and justice will come.
rationales.B: Stowe writes for the enslaved, not for their masters; her morning belongs to the just, and the evil faces an eternal night.
rationales.C: The passage is a moral claim, not a disclaimer; Stowe judges slavery, not by calling it make-believe.
rationales.D: Background from the books: Stowe wrote to make Northerners feel slavery’s cruelty; the passage urges them on, it does not send them away.
rationales.general:
1. Follow the image: the longest way must have its close, the gloomiest night wears on to morning.
2. Ask who the morning belongs to: the just, while the day of evil ends in night.
3. Name the belief: slavery will not last forever; justice is coming.
Remember: a novel’s closing lines often state its moral outright; read them as the author’s verdict.
